sources.quote: I was born/ he writes, 'on Sept. 27, 1920, in Wilmington, Delaware.
Henry Stommel's heart stopped beating shortly after midnight on Friday, January 17, 1992, four days after he had undergone surgery for liver cancer at Deaconess Hospital in Brookline, Massachusetts.
As an undergraduate at Yale he had been advised by a counselor that, since he evidently had no talent for science, he should take up law.
When Hank arrived at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in 1944 there was little reason to suppose that anything momentous had taken place.
By this time, Henry had moved back to Woods Hole from MIT.
When I was called to the chair of oceanography at Harvard, it was only after Walter had declined it.
After he and Elizabeth (Chickie) Brown were married in 1950, they frequently entertained visiting oceanographers...
In 1955, when he was invited by Jule Charney to visit the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, he and I worked on a problem together...
He initiated studies in double diffusion, first with Arnold Arons and Duncan Blanchard (the salt fountain)...
But the development of GFD began in earnest in the mid-1950s when Stommel and Malkus spearheaded a joint seminar between WHOI and MIT...
Hank and I collaborated (with Bernard Haurwitz) on a spectral analysis of 10 years of Bermuda offshore temperature data...
Editor's Note: Allan Robinson and Henry Stommel co-directed the Mid-Ocean Dynamics Experiment and and were co-chairmen of the US POLYMODE Organizing Committee.

I had the Scripps vessel, Argo, for two cruises of three months each in 1962 and 1963... and Henry thought it would be an excellent opportunity for some of his theoretical colleagues to see how the other half lived.
Hank sent one of his better MIT students, Carl Wunsch, to work with me during winter of 1965 to 1966.
With it he collaborated often with Jim Luyten and more recently with Xin Huang on a variety of simple dynamical models...
...and in the past few years he and Nelson Hogg explored the representation of heat flux in terms of point baroclinic vortices.
As Stern talked, I quickly grasped that he had quite independently developed a new theory, that of double-diffusive convection.

We started to work on the thermocline problem with Jim Luyten. Jim and Hank had already begun some numerical studies of the ventilated thermocline, and I was able to find a verifying analytical solution...

We have also chosen to include unpublished pieces of Hank's writing about science, as well as some of his contributions to the Falmouth, Massachusetts, newspaper The Enterprise, under his nom de plume, Starbuck.
Over a three-week period he wrote a 208-page book, Science of the Seven Seas, which was published by Cornell Maritime Press in 1945.
He based an introductory course about ocean circulation on a set of programs that he wrote for his book, A View of the Sea, published in 1989.
In 1980 the Stommels coauthored Volcano Weather, the Stonj of 1816, the Year Without a Summer.
